titre: A Man Swears He Never Met Don Quixote
accroche: In the true sequel to Don Quixote, a character swears he never crossed paths with the hero. Cervantes was settling scores with a forger.
contenu_vulgarise:
In the last third of the true second part of Don Quixote, the alcalde of a village, a local magistrate, records a statement in due and proper form. A certain Don Álvaro Tarfe swears solemnly there that he has never met Don Quixote of La Mancha or his squire Sancho Panza, and that he has nothing to do with what a book published under the name of a certain Avellaneda makes him say. The scene is absurd: a fictional character signs, before a magistrate who is also fictional, a document attesting that a third work of fiction lies. It nevertheless targets a very real target.

## A Stolen Sequel, an Answer Written Inside It

In 1614, while Cervantes is still working on the true second part of his novel, a book appears under the title Segundo tomo del ingenioso hidalgo don Quijote de la Mancha, signed “Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda,” a name no one has ever been able to identify with certainty. Its preface writer attacks Cervantes directly, then sixty-seven years old and maimed in one hand since the Battle of Lepanto, two details Avellaneda turns into mockery. Cervantes addresses it from the opening of his own book: “By God! With what impatience, illustrious reader, or perhaps plebeian, you must now await this prologue, believing you will find in it vengeances, quarrels, outrageous reproaches to the author of the second Don Quixote!”

Rather than settling for an indignant preface, Cervantes brings the fake into the real. In chapter 59, his own Don Quixote learns of the existence of Avellaneda's book and changes route so as not to prove it right. Then, in chapter 72, he meets Tarfe, a character borrowed as is from the rival book, and persuades him to have the local alcalde record, in due and proper form, that he has never met him. A character of Cervantes thus has Avellaneda's book officially refuted by a character of Avellaneda's.

## A Death That Closes the File for Good

Cervantes goes further still. Two chapters before the end, his hero regains his reason on his deathbed, renounces chivalry, dictates his will, then dies surrounded by his own. The priest even has a notarial attestation drawn up certifying “that Alonzo Quijano the Good, commonly called Don Quixote of La Mancha, had passed from this life into the other, and died naturally,” the text specifies, to “remove any pretext for an author other than Cid Hamet Ben-Engeli to falsely resurrect him.” Cervantes's readers see in it a direct answer to Avellaneda: a character who could be brought back to life in a fake book as long as he remained alive in the real one. Dead and buried, notarial act in support, Don Quixote could no longer be stolen.

carte.punch: In Don Quixote, a character swears under oath that he never met... Don Quixote.
carte.idee: Furious over a fake sequel published in 1614, Cervantes slips into his true second part a character from the fake book, whom he has swear before the village alcalde that he never met his hero, before having Don Quixote die, notarial act in support.

quiz.question: Why does Cervantes have Don Quixote die, notarial act in support, at the end of his novel?
choix: To respect an editorial convention of the time requiring every chivalric romance to end with a death
To prevent anyone, after Avellaneda's fake sequel, from still resurrecting the character in another fake book
Because the historical figure who inspired Don Quixote had actually died that year
To honor the wishes of his publisher, who refused to fund a third part
quiz.explication: No convention required this ending, and Don Quixote is not the biography of a real person. No publisher's refusal is documented either. Cervantes says it almost explicitly through the priest: the notarial act aims to prevent another author from falsely resurrecting the character. It is a direct response to Avellaneda, whose fake sequel of 1614 had enraged him.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do we know about the identity of the author of the fake sequel published in 1614?
choix: He is a declared rival of Cervantes, well identified
He is a former secretary of Cervantes dismissed in 1610
He signs under the name Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda, an identity never established with certainty
He publishes under his real name, known to historians since the eighteenth century
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1614 book is signed Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda, a name no one has ever been able to identify with certainty, despite the many hypotheses advanced since.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which two personal details of Cervantes does Avellaneda's preface writer mock?
choix: His age, sixty-seven, and his hand wounded at the Battle of Lepanto
His poverty and his inability to find a publisher
His forced exile and his ignorance of Castilian
His partial blindness and his inability to finish his novels
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The preface writer of the fake sequel mocks Cervantes's age, then sixty-seven, and his hand wounded at the Battle of Lepanto, two real details of his life.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What exactly does Don Álvaro Tarfe do in chapter 72 of the true second part?
choix: He fights Don Quixote in a duel to clear his honor
He becomes Don Quixote's new squire in place of Sancho
He publishes a retraction himself in a pamphlet distributed in Madrid
He swears before the village alcalde that he has never met Don Quixote or Sancho Panza
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cervantes has Tarfe, a character borrowed from Avellaneda's book, make a statement before the village alcalde and a clerk, affirming that he never met Don Quixote or Sancho Panza.
